is a hybrid streaming platform. Apache Kafka is used as the ingestion framework to capture text messages from various sources (Twitter API, news RSS, e-commerce reviews, among others). Kafka’s fault-tolerant, partitioned queues ensure messages are not lost under heavy traffic (
) [5]. Data producers attach metadata (timestamp, source, location) to each message and publish to Kafka topics.

Apache Flink is the engine responsible for real-time processing. Flink jobs consume from Kafka in an event-driven manner [1]. Flink stream operators perform real-time transformations: preprocessing that cleans text (lowercasing, anti-spam filters, URL expansion), tokenization, and language detection (for example using
). Filters for deduplication eliminate retweets and duplicate reviews.
Each processed message is fed into a sentiment analysis operator containing a transformer model (

) fine-tuned on sentiment classification [4]. The model is refactored into an optimized inference engine using ONNX Runtime to provide low latency [9]. If a message is in a non-English language, Flink routes it to a multilingual model or performs automatic translation [6]. The transformer outputs a sentiment label and confidence score. The result is a stream of (timestamp,

, metadata) tuples ingested into a real-time analytics backend or time-series database. A dashboard (Apache Superset or Grafana) plots sentiment trends across time and geography. Superset is designed to handle real-time analytics workloads (Preset.io) [7].

For the collection of the data from diverse sources we used Apache Kafka. For example, the Twitter Streaming API is used to fetch the tweets which are then published to a Kafka topic. News articles and customer reviews are similarly pushed into Kafka. Since Kafka has high throughput, it ensures that no record is left behind even during traffic spikes. In Flink, multiple consumer groups can scale horizontally to match the data rate [5][1].
Flink jobs consume the raw text from Kafka. Cleaning and tokenization are the first steps that include removing HTML tags, punctuation,

, and splitting into tokens; for this, regular expressions or NLP libraries are used. After this, a language detection module is used to label the text’s language. Messages which are non-English are flagged for separate handling (for example, translation or use of a multilingual model). A faux detector (Bloom filter tracking seen tweet IDs) filters out reposted content in order to reduce redundancy. We also performed named-entity recognition to tag proper nouns. This pipeline is implemented as chained Flink operators for efficiency [1][6].

, a new system that does real-time sentiment analysis on massive data streams. It combines Apache Kafka for ingestion, Apache Flink for low-latency stream processing, and a set of lightweight transformer models for NLP to create a system that can provide a real-time view of the sentiment of a massive data stream, without the batch latency associated with traditional systems [1][3][5][10]. Our contributions include a hybrid streaming architecture, a lightweight inference pipeline that uses distilled models for inference, and an interactive analytics dashboard [4][7][11][12]. In simulated experiments, we show that

can process high volume social streams with low latency and produce actionable insights far more quickly than traditional batch-based systems [1][8][10]. Real-time sentiment intelligence is increasingly important in domains

such as finance (stock market reaction), marketing (campaign monitoring), and public health (public concern tracking) [2][6][11]. As data continues to grow and real-time awareness becomes more valuable,
hybrid streaming approach highlights the importance of integrating time-sensitive streaming infrastructure with modern AI models to produce timely sentiment trends [1][5][9][10].

We intend to investigate the possibility of using large language models (e.g. GPT-4) for not just polarity
(anger, joy, fear). LLMs could also provide better context for
examples and could summarize sentiment trends (e.g. summarizing why sentiment spiked) [6][11][12].
The analytics could be expanded to include a geographic component. If location is available,

could produce heat maps of sentiment by city or region in real-time. Related work notes that big data sentiment analysis can handle multiple languages and locales with ease (numerous.ai) [2][11], which we would use. Also, topic clustering algorithms could be used to identify new topics of conversation as they arise in real-time [3][10].

Online learning could be used to allow the sentiment model to adapt to new slang or domain shifts. For example, when a new product is launched the system could learn its context quickly from incoming data [1][11].
In future work we will conduct larger benchmarks, including other frameworks [5][10].

We plan to integrate other data streaming algorithms (e.g. Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming), as well as other hardware (GPU, FPGA) in order to improve the latency/accuracy trade-offs [5][9][10]. This would help us extend
coverage to the complete set of public sentiment that exists across modalities, languages, and regions [2][6][11].
